subtopic_detail: Discriminating substance induced psychosis from a primary psychotic disorder
stem:
You are the on call psychiatry registrar reviewing a 22 year old man in the emergency department overnight. Police brought him in for bizarre behaviour at a house party. He is agitated, expressing paranoid beliefs that his housemates have been replaced by identical imposters. He describes third person auditory hallucinations telling him to leave the city. Collateral from his mother reports he has been smoking increasing amounts of high potency cannabis over the last 3 months, most recently daily. He has no prior psychiatric history documented. There is no family history of schizophrenia. He denies other drug use.

Urine drug screen is positive only for cannabis (delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol metabolites). He has been observed in a single room for the last 6 hours and remains highly paranoid without change. He is medically stable. Consent for admission has been obtained via a temporary treatment order under the state mental health act.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.0 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, oriented, tangential thought form, paranoid delusions, auditory hallucinations third person, no cognitive impairment on brief bedside cognitive test
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for cannabinoids only, full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, thyroid function, C reactive protein within normal limits, computed tomography head normal

lead_in: What is the most important clinical feature that discriminates cannabis induced psychotic disorder from a primary psychotic disorder here?

options.text: Persistence of psychotic symptoms beyond 1 month of confirmed cannabis abstinence points to a primary psychotic disorder
options.rationale: The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual 5th edition Text Revision requires cannabis induced psychotic disorder symptoms to remit within about 1 month of confirmed abstinence; persistence beyond that supports a primary psychotic disorder such as first episode schizophrenia. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.text: Presence of paranoid delusions alone confirms a primary psychotic disorder rather than substance induced psychosis
options.rationale: Paranoid delusions occur in both cannabis induced psychosis and primary psychotic disorders; the delusion type alone is not discriminatory. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.text: Third person auditory hallucinations are pathognomonic of schizophrenia and rule out cannabis induced psychosis
options.rationale: Third person auditory hallucinations are suggestive of schizophrenia (first rank symptom) but occur in substance induced psychosis and are not pathognomonic. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.text: A urine drug screen positive for delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol metabolites confirms cannabis induced psychosis
options.rationale: A positive urine cannabinoid screen reflects recent use only and does not confirm causation; delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol metabolites can persist for weeks and coexist with a primary psychotic disorder. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.text: The absence of family history of schizophrenia rules out a primary psychotic disorder in a young adult
options.rationale: Family history is a risk factor but its absence does not rule out first episode psychosis. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

explanation.summary: Distinguishing cannabis induced psychotic disorder from a primary psychotic disorder rests principally on temporal association: symptoms in the substance induced condition are expected to resolve within around a month of confirmed abstinence, whereas persistence beyond that points toward a primary disorder such as first episode schizophrenia. Symptom content, family history, and urine drug screen positivity are supportive but not discriminatory. A short assertive follow up with abstinence support, brief antipsychotic (e.g. olanzapine 5 to 10 mg) and psychoeducation, then reassessment at 4 to 6 weeks is the standard AU approach. Suicide risk assessment is essential because self harm risk is high in first episode psychosis.
key_points: Cannabis induced psychosis remits within around 1 month of confirmed abstinence.
Persistence beyond a month with confirmed abstinence supports a primary psychotic disorder.
Follow up at 4 to 6 weeks with abstinence support is essential regardless of the initial classification.
explanation.pearls: Persistence of psychosis beyond one month of confirmed cannabis abstinence tips the diagnosis from substance induced to a primary psychotic disorder.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders
Diagnostic and Statistical Manual 5th edition Text Revision

subtopic_detail: First line psychological therapy for post traumatic stress disorder
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 36 year old former soldier who returned from deployment 2 years ago. He describes intrusive memories of a specific vehicle borne improvised explosive device incident, distressing nightmares 3 to 4 times per week, hypervigilance when driving, and avoidance of crowded shopping centres. He drinks 6 to 8 standard drinks daily to sleep and has not worked for 6 months. He denies current suicidal intent but has ongoing passive thoughts of not wanting to be alive. He is not psychotic. He has never had structured psychological therapy. He has been on sertraline 100 mg for 6 months with only partial improvement in mood.

He is engaged and asks what specific psychological therapy would be most helpful. He has private health insurance and can access accredited psychologists.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 /min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, dysphoric, no thought disorder, no psychomotor slowing, no cognitive impairment
data_table.Investigations: Kessler 10 score 32, PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 score 62; full blood count, liver function tests and urea and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: Which psychological therapy has the strongest first line evidence for post traumatic stress disorder in AU adult veterans?

options.text: Supportive psychotherapy weekly for 12 sessions delivered by a general counsellor with mental health experience
options.rationale: Supportive psychotherapy is not first line; trauma focused psychotherapies have stronger evidence and are preferred first line. (Source: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, Post Traumatic Stress Disorder and Complex Post Traumatic Stress Disorder)
source_refs: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, Post Traumatic Stress Disorder and Complex Post Traumatic Stress Disorder

options.text: Trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing as first line therapy
options.rationale: The Australian guidelines recommend trauma focused psychological therapies (trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy including prolonged exposure and cognitive processing therapy, or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing) as first line for post traumatic stress disorder in adults, including veterans. (Source: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, Post Traumatic Stress Disorder and Complex Post Traumatic Stress Disorder)
source_refs: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, Post Traumatic Stress Disorder and Complex Post Traumatic Stress Disorder

options.text: Psychodynamic psychotherapy weekly for 12 months delivered by an accredited psychodynamic psychotherapist locally
options.rationale: Psychodynamic psychotherapy is not first line for post traumatic stress disorder in the Australian guidelines; trauma focused therapies are preferred. (Source: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, Post Traumatic Stress Disorder and Complex Post Traumatic Stress Disorder)
source_refs: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, Post Traumatic Stress Disorder and Complex Post Traumatic Stress Disorder

options.text: Group interpersonal therapy alone delivered by an accredited practitioner for the recommended 12 week programme
options.rationale: Group interpersonal therapy is not first line for post traumatic stress disorder; trauma focused psychological therapy delivered individually is preferred. (Source: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, Post Traumatic Stress Disorder and Complex Post Traumatic Stress Disorder)
source_refs: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, Post Traumatic Stress Disorder and Complex Post Traumatic Stress Disorder

options.text: Mindfulness based stress reduction as sole therapy delivered by an accredited practitioner for the 8 week programme
options.rationale: Mindfulness based stress reduction is not first line; it can be used adjunctively but not in place of trauma focused therapy. (Source: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, Post Traumatic Stress Disorder and Complex Post Traumatic Stress Disorder)
source_refs: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, Post Traumatic Stress Disorder and Complex Post Traumatic Stress Disorder

explanation.summary: The Australian guidelines for post traumatic stress disorder recommend trauma focused psychological therapies as first line for adults, including prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy (both under the trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy umbrella) and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and venlafaxine are first line pharmacological options when psychotherapy is declined, unavailable or inadequate. Comorbid alcohol use disorder often requires concurrent management. Adjunctive supports include sleep hygiene, exercise, and treatment of comorbid depression and pain. Referral to accredited psychologists trained in these modalities is essential.
key_points: First line psychotherapy in adult post traumatic stress disorder: trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing.
First line pharmacotherapy where psychotherapy is not chosen or inadequate: selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor or venlafaxine.
Address comorbid alcohol use disorder concurrently.
explanation.pearls: Adult post traumatic stress disorder: refer for trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing; sertraline is a pharmacological adjunct.

sources.label: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, Post Traumatic Stress Disorder and Complex Post Traumatic Stress Disorder
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Post Traumatic Stress Disorder

subtopic_detail: Opportunistic infection prophylaxis thresholds in newly diagnosed HIV
stem:
You are the infectious diseases registrar reviewing a 32 year old man with newly diagnosed HIV. He presented with 2 weeks of dry cough, exertional dyspnoea and 4 kg weight loss. He is now hospitalised. His viral load is 380,000 copies/mL and his CD4 count returned this afternoon. Chest X ray shows bilateral diffuse interstitial infiltrates. He has been started on treatment doses of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for suspected Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia after bronchoalveolar lavage. Toxoplasma IgG is positive. Cytomegalovirus IgG positive.

He has never taken antiretroviral therapy. The infectious diseases consultant is planning to start dolutegravir plus tenofovir alafenamide and emtricitabine after 2 weeks. He asks what other prophylactic antimicrobials to start now given the CD4 result.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 106 /min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 /min, SpO2 92% on 2 L nasal prongs, temperature 38.4 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, mucosal candidiasis, fine crackles bilaterally, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: CD4 count 42 cells/microL, viral load 380,000 copies/mL, toxoplasma IgG positive, cytomegalovirus IgG positive, cryptococcal antigen negative

lead_in: Which opportunistic infection prophylaxis regimen best matches ASHM guidance for this CD4 count?

options.text: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double strength daily for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis only at this point in his HIV care
options.rationale: At CD4 below 100 with positive toxoplasma serology, the trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole regimen also covers toxoplasmosis and no additional agent is required for toxoplasmosis, but Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis is separately considered. (Source: ASHM HIV Management in Australasia)
source_refs: ASHM HIV Management in Australasia

options.text: Fluconazole 200 mg daily for oral candidiasis treatment and primary cryptococcosis prevention at this point in his HIV care today
options.rationale: Primary fluconazole prophylaxis is not routinely recommended without positive cryptococcal antigen or symptomatic disease; treat the candidiasis if symptomatic. (Source: ASHM HIV Management in Australasia)
source_refs: ASHM HIV Management in Australasia

options.text: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double strength daily (covers Pneumocystis and toxoplasmosis) plus azithromycin 1200 mg weekly for MAC prophylaxis
options.rationale: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double strength daily covers Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and, at CD4 below 100 with toxoplasma seropositivity, toxoplasmosis. Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis with azithromycin 1200 mg weekly is considered at CD4 below 50 (historical threshold; modern guidance recognises many regions now defer if antiretroviral therapy is imminent, but the threshold and agent remain examinable). (Source: ASHM HIV Management in Australasia)
source_refs: ASHM HIV Management in Australasia

options.text: Isoniazid 300 mg daily for 9 months regardless of tuberculosis screening result, given the low CD4 count at this presentation today
options.rationale: Isoniazid preventive therapy is guided by tuberculosis screening (QuantiFERON tuberculosis Gold Plus or tuberculin skin test) and country of origin risk; it is not started without a screen result. (Source: ASHM HIV Management in Australasia)
source_refs: ASHM HIV Management in Australasia

options.text: Valganciclovir 900 mg daily for primary cytomegalovirus prophylaxis given the positive cytomegalovirus IgG serology reported today
options.rationale: Primary cytomegalovirus prophylaxis is not routinely recommended in AU; commence after cytomegalovirus retinitis is diagnosed or high viral load on quantitative polymerase chain reaction. (Source: ASHM HIV Management in Australasia)
source_refs: ASHM HIV Management in Australasia

explanation.summary: Australian HIV opportunistic infection prophylaxis is anchored by CD4 threshold. At CD4 below 200, start trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia; at CD4 below 100 with positive toxoplasma serology, the same trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole regimen covers toxoplasmosis. At CD4 below 50, azithromycin 1200 mg weekly for Mycobacterium avium complex is the traditional prophylaxis (modern guidance in some regions defers if antiretroviral therapy is imminent and reliably tolerated). Primary cryptococcal, cytomegalovirus and antituberculous prophylaxis are guided by antigen, quantitative polymerase chain reaction and tuberculosis screening respectively. Prophylaxis can be discontinued after immune reconstitution.
key_points: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis threshold CD4 <200; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
Toxoplasma prophylaxis threshold CD4 <100 with positive toxoplasma IgG; same trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole covers both.
Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis threshold CD4 <50; azithromycin 1200 mg weekly.
explanation.pearls: CD4 42 cells/microL with toxoplasma IgG positive: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double strength daily covers Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and toxoplasmosis; add azithromycin 1200 mg weekly for Mycobacterium avium complex.

sources.label: ASHM HIV Management in Australasia
US DHHS Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Opportunistic Infections in Adults and Adolescents with HIV

stem:
You are the general medicine registrar admitting a 68 year old woman from the emergency department with community acquired pneumonia progressing to septic shock. She has a 3 day history of productive cough, fever and dyspnoea. She has type 2 diabetes on metformin and hypertension on perindopril. She is now confused (Glasgow Coma Score 13). Sepsis screen has been in progress for 30 minutes. Blood cultures, lactate and lung imaging are done. Intravenous access has been obtained peripherally. She is on 6 L nasal oxygen.

Ward rounds have paused; her nurse asks what to give next in the first hour. Chest X ray shows a right lower lobe consolidation and small effusion. She has no penicillin allergy. No known reason to withhold intravenous crystalloid.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 84/48 mmHg (mean arterial pressure 60 mmHg), respiratory rate 28 /min, SpO2 92% on 6 L nasal prongs, temperature 38.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Confused, Glasgow Coma Score 13, right basal crackles, cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 s
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 145 micromol/L (baseline 78), white cell count 18 x10^9/L, C reactive protein 260 mg/L, procalcitonin 4.2 microg/L

lead_in: Which combination of interventions best matches the Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle in AU?

options.text: Broad spectrum antibiotics within 3 hours, 500 mL crystalloid over 60 minutes, lactate remeasured at 6 hours from presentation
options.rationale: Antibiotics should be within 1 hour in septic shock (not 3), initial fluid target is 30 mL/kg not 500 mL, and lactate is remeasured within 2 hours. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines 2021)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines 2021

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g monotherapy, no fluid until vasopressor commenced, mean arterial pressure target 65 mmHg or above
options.rationale: Fluid resuscitation precedes vasopressor unless volume overload is present, and coverage for atypical or resistant pathogens should be considered in shocked pneumonia per Therapeutic Guidelines. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines 2021)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines 2021

options.text: Intravenous amoxicillin plus gentamicin, 10 mL/kg fluid bolus over 60 minutes, wait for lactate to fall before adjusting therapy
options.rationale: Amoxicillin plus gentamicin does not adequately cover severe community acquired pneumonia; 10 mL/kg is below Surviving Sepsis Campaign 30 mL/kg starting fluid; lactate should be re measured within 2 hours. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines 2021)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines 2021

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g plus azithromycin 500 mg within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid, noradrenaline to mean arterial 65
options.rationale: The AU adaptation of the Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle in severe community acquired pneumonia is empirical ceftriaxone 1 g intravenous plus azithromycin 500 mg intravenous (Therapeutic Guidelines) within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid within 3 hours, noradrenaline titrated to mean arterial pressure 65 mmHg if fluid unresponsive, and lactate reassessed within 2 hours; peripheral vasopressor via a proximal large bore line is acceptable while central access is arranged. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines 2021)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines 2021

options.text: Intravenous meropenem 1 g monotherapy, 20 mL/kg saline over 30 minutes, target mean arterial pressure 75 mmHg from noradrenaline
options.rationale: Meropenem is not first line empirical therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia in AU; mean arterial pressure target is 65 mmHg by default; 20 mL/kg is below the 30 mL/kg starting fluid target. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines 2021)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines 2021

explanation.summary: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle requires measurement of lactate (and re measurement within 2 hours if elevated), blood cultures before antibiotics if this does not delay them, broad spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour of recognition in septic shock, and 30 mL/kg intravenous balanced crystalloid within 3 hours in shock or lactate above 4 mmol/L. Vasopressor with noradrenaline first line targets a mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg. Empirical antibiotics for severe community acquired pneumonia in AU per Therapeutic Guidelines are intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Peripheral vasopressor via a proximal large bore vein is acceptable while central access is arranged.
key_points: Antibiotics within 1 hour in septic shock; empirical severe community acquired pneumonia cover is ceftriaxone plus azithromycin in AU.
30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid within 3 hours; re measure lactate within 2 hours.
Noradrenaline first line; target mean arterial pressure 65 mmHg.
explanation.pearls: Septic shock hour-1 bundle in severe community acquired pneumonia: ceftriaxone plus azithromycin within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg fluid, noradrenaline to mean arterial pressure 65 mmHg, repeat lactate at 2 hours.

sources.label: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines 2021
Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Community acquired pneumonia

subtopic_detail: Tension pneumothorax vs primary spontaneous pneumothorax management pathway
stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar attending a 22 year old tall thin man who presented with sudden left sided pleuritic chest pain and mild dyspnoea while sitting studying. He is not hypoxic, tolerating conversation and haemodynamically stable. There is no trauma. His symptoms started 2 hours ago and are worse on deep inspiration. He has no prior lung disease. He is a light social smoker. Chest X ray done 30 minutes ago shows a left sided pneumothorax with an intrapleural distance of 2 cm at the level of the hilum, no mediastinal shift, no surgical emphysema.

He is comfortable now. There is no clinical evidence of tension. His observations have been stable for 30 minutes on room air.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Reduced breath sounds left upper zone, resonant to percussion, no tracheal deviation, no jugular venous distension
data_table.Investigations: Chest X ray left pneumothorax with 2 cm intrapleural distance at hilum, no mediastinal shift, no other lung pathology; blood gases not done

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Immediate needle thoracostomy at the second intercostal space midclavicular line with a 14 gauge cannula on the affected side
options.rationale: Needle thoracostomy is reserved for tension pneumothorax with cardiovascular compromise; this patient is stable and does not have signs of tension. (Source: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline)
source_refs: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline

options.text: Insert an intercostal catheter 28 French to underwater seal drain in the fifth intercostal space anterior axillary line
options.rationale: Large bore chest drain is not first line for primary spontaneous pneumothorax that is not compromising the patient; smaller bore drainage or aspiration is preferred in the current pathway if intervention is needed. (Source: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline)
source_refs: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline

options.text: Discharge home with paracetamol as needed and no imaging follow up because he is now clinically asymptomatic at rest
options.rationale: A pneumothorax of this size needs at least clinical observation, oxygen if hypoxic and follow up imaging; discharge without follow up is inappropriate. (Source: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline)
source_refs: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline

options.text: Commence high flow nasal cannula at 40 L/min to accelerate pleural air reabsorption over the next 24 hours on ward
options.rationale: Supplemental oxygen (nasal prong or non rebreather) is used to speed pleural air reabsorption in a small pneumothorax under observation, not high flow nasal cannula; hospital admission with supplemental oxygen is the pathway. (Source: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline)
source_refs: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline

options.text: Admit for observation with supplemental oxygen; if breathless or the pneumothorax progresses use needle aspiration first
options.rationale: For a primary spontaneous pneumothorax over 2 cm in a symptomatic but stable patient, current British Thoracic Society and modern conservative pathway favours admission with observation and supplemental oxygen. Intervention (needle aspiration first line, small bore drain if aspiration fails) is reserved for breathlessness, progression or failure of conservative therapy. Ambulatory management with a Heimlich style device is a modern option in appropriate centres. (Source: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline)
source_refs: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline

explanation.summary: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax management is determined by symptoms rather than radiological size alone in current guidelines. A stable, only mildly symptomatic patient is admitted for observation and supplemental oxygen (which accelerates pleural air reabsorption). Intervention is needle aspiration first line (14 to 16 gauge cannula in the second intercostal space midclavicular line, up to 2.5 L drawn), progressing to a small bore chest drain (8 to 14 French) if aspiration fails. Tension pneumothorax with cardiovascular compromise is treated with immediate needle decompression. Ambulatory management with a Heimlich style device is a modern option in select centres.
key_points: Needle thoracostomy is only for tension pneumothorax with cardiovascular compromise.
Primary spontaneous pneumothorax with symptoms: needle aspiration first line, small bore drain if aspiration fails.
Supplemental oxygen (nasal prong or non rebreather) speeds pleural air reabsorption.
explanation.pearls: A stable primary spontaneous pneumothorax over 2 cm with mild symptoms is admitted for observation and oxygen; intervention (needle aspiration first, small bore drain if fails) is for breathlessness or progression.

sources.label: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline
Therapeutic Guidelines Respiratory: Pneumothorax

subtopic_detail: First line biochemical test for suspected Cushing syndrome
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 46 year old woman referred by her general practitioner with 12 months of central weight gain, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness, dorsocervical fat pad and abdominal purple striae. Her blood pressure is 168/98 mmHg on ramipril 10 mg and amlodipine 10 mg. She has type 2 diabetes diagnosed 8 months ago on metformin 1 g twice daily with haemoglobin A1c 9.8 percent. She has never taken oral, inhaled, injected or topical corticosteroids. She drinks 2 standard drinks per week and has no history of depression. Her menstrual cycle is regular. She is not pregnant. Family history is unremarkable.

Blood pressure logs at home confirm sustained hypertension. She has not had prior investigation for Cushing syndrome. Her weight is stable now and she is compliant with her medications.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86 /min, blood pressure 168/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Dorsocervical fat pad, wide purple abdominal striae, proximal muscle weakness (30 s sit to stand test 6 repetitions), thin skin
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 9.4 mmol/L, potassium 3.4 mmol/L, haemoglobin A1c 9.8 percent, spot cortisol 8am 720 nmol/L (140-690)

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first line screening test?

options.text: 24 hour urinary free cortisol collection on two separate 24 hour collections over the coming two weeks in outpatients
options.rationale: The Endocrine Society and Australian guidance advise 3 first line screens for Cushing syndrome that can be used interchangeably or in combination: 24 hour urinary free cortisol on 2 collections, 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test, and late night salivary cortisol (2 samples). Any single positive screen is followed by a second modality. This is the most appropriate first line screening option among those listed. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Random daytime serum cortisol level only, on a single blood sample sent from clinic without additional confirmation
options.rationale: Random daytime serum cortisol is confounded by pulsatile secretion, stress and time of day; it is not a first line screen for Cushing syndrome. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Serum adrenocorticotropic hormone at 8 am alone, on a single blood sample sent from clinic without additional test
options.rationale: Serum adrenocorticotropic hormone is used to localise cause after Cushing syndrome is biochemically confirmed, not as a first line screen. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Contrast enhanced computed tomography of the pituitary alone as a first line screening investigation from clinic today
options.rationale: Imaging is used after biochemical confirmation and localisation; it is not first line for screening. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: High dose (8 mg) dexamethasone suppression test alone as first line screening investigation for suspected Cushing today
options.rationale: High dose 8 mg dexamethasone suppression test is a localising test used after confirmation, not a first line screen. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Cushing syndrome is confirmed biochemically before imaging. The three first line screens are 24 hour urinary free cortisol (2 collections), 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (post dose cortisol below 50 nmol/L excludes Cushing), and late night salivary cortisol (2 samples). At least two abnormal tests are typically required to confirm. Adrenocorticotropic hormone, high dose dexamethasone suppression test, corticotropin releasing hormone stimulation test and imaging (pituitary magnetic resonance imaging or adrenal computed tomography) are localising tests used after confirmation. Cyclical Cushing syndrome and exogenous glucocorticoid exposure are common confounders in initial workup.
key_points: Three first line screens for Cushing syndrome: 24 hour urinary free cortisol, 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression, late night salivary cortisol.
Adrenocorticotropic hormone, imaging and high dose dexamethasone suppression are localising steps after confirmation.
Exclude exogenous glucocorticoid exposure before investigation.
explanation.pearls: First line Cushing screening: 24 hour urinary free cortisol on 2 collections (or 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression, or late night salivary cortisol). Do not order pituitary imaging or adrenocorticotropic hormone as the first test.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline
Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Adrenal disorders

subtopic_detail: Multiple sclerosis: dissemination in time and space criteria
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 28 year old woman referred for right sided visual blurring and pain on eye movement for 4 days. She had a similar episode 8 months ago (right hand clumsiness for 10 days) which resolved without treatment. Neurological examination now demonstrates a right relative afferent pupillary defect and mildly reduced visual acuity in the right eye (6/12) with normal fields on confrontation. There is no other focal neurology today.

A magnetic resonance imaging brain and spinal cord with gadolinium has been performed on referral. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis has been sent and shows unmatched oligoclonal bands. She has no other medical history and takes no medication. She lives alone and is asking about whether she has multiple sclerosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 /min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Right relative afferent pupillary defect, right visual acuity 6/12, no other cranial nerve deficit, tone power and coordination intact
data_table.Investigations: Magnetic resonance imaging: two T2 hyperintense lesions periventricular (one enhancing with gadolinium), one non enhancing juxtacortical lesion, one non enhancing cord lesion at C4. Cerebrospinal fluid: unmatched oligoclonal bands, cell count 4, protein 0.48 g/L (0.15-0.45)

lead_in: Do the current findings meet the 2017 McDonald criteria for relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis?

options.text: No, criteria require a third clinical attack with objective evidence in a new central nervous system location before diagnosis
options.rationale: McDonald 2017 does not require three clinical attacks; two clinical attacks with objective evidence of two lesions in dissemination in space suffices, and dissemination in time can be met by magnetic resonance imaging or cerebrospinal fluid oligoclonal bands. (Source: 2017 McDonald Criteria for Multiple Sclerosis)
source_refs: 2017 McDonald Criteria for Multiple Sclerosis

options.text: Yes, two clinical attacks with objective evidence, dissemination in space (multiple sites) and simultaneous enhancing plus non enhancing lesions meet criteria
options.rationale: McDonald 2017: two clinical attacks and objective evidence of two lesions with clinical localisation to two areas of the central nervous system satisfies dissemination in space. Simultaneous presence of enhancing and non enhancing lesions on a single magnetic resonance imaging (or a new T2/enhancing lesion on follow up) satisfies dissemination in time. Cerebrospinal fluid unmatched oligoclonal bands can substitute for dissemination in time. All criteria are met here. (Source: 2017 McDonald Criteria for Multiple Sclerosis)
source_refs: 2017 McDonald Criteria for Multiple Sclerosis

options.text: No, spinal cord lesions are not accepted in McDonald 2017 for dissemination in space in an initial diagnostic assessment
options.rationale: Spinal cord lesions are accepted as dissemination in space in McDonald 2017 and can substitute for infratentorial location. (Source: 2017 McDonald Criteria for Multiple Sclerosis)
source_refs: 2017 McDonald Criteria for Multiple Sclerosis

options.text: No, both attacks must be within 30 days of each other for the McDonald 2017 criteria to be considered met at this stage
options.rationale: Attacks are defined as at least 24 hours in duration and must occur at least 30 days apart, not within 30 days; two attacks 8 months apart are separate. (Source: 2017 McDonald Criteria for Multiple Sclerosis)
source_refs: 2017 McDonald Criteria for Multiple Sclerosis

options.text: No, aquaporin 4 antibody testing must be documented negative before the McDonald 2017 diagnosis can be given at this stage
options.rationale: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder should be considered in atypical or high suspicion cases (particularly bilateral or severe optic neuritis or transverse myelitis) but aquaporin 4 testing is not a mandated part of the McDonald 2017 criteria in typical cases. (Source: 2017 McDonald Criteria for Multiple Sclerosis)
source_refs: 2017 McDonald Criteria for Multiple Sclerosis

explanation.summary: The 2017 McDonald criteria diagnose relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis from a combination of clinical attacks, objective evidence of central nervous system lesions and dissemination in space and time. Two clinical attacks with objective evidence of two lesions or one lesion with reasonable historical evidence of a prior attack satisfies dissemination in space. Dissemination in time can be satisfied by simultaneous presence of enhancing and non enhancing lesions on magnetic resonance imaging, a new T2 or enhancing lesion on follow up, or a second clinical attack; cerebrospinal fluid unmatched oligoclonal bands can substitute for dissemination in time. Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (aquaporin 4 antibody) and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody disease should be considered in atypical presentations before disease modifying therapy.
key_points: Dissemination in space: >=2 lesions across periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, or spinal cord.
Dissemination in time: simultaneous enhancing and non enhancing lesions, or new lesion on follow up, or a second clinical attack, or unmatched cerebrospinal fluid oligoclonal bands.
Consider neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody disease in atypical presentations.
explanation.pearls: Two clinical attacks 8 months apart with simultaneous enhancing and non enhancing lesions across periventricular, juxtacortical and cord regions plus oligoclonal bands meets McDonald 2017.

sources.label: 2017 McDonald Criteria for Multiple Sclerosis
MS Australia Clinical Guidelines for Diagnosis and Management of Multiple Sclerosis

subtopic_detail: Pattern recognition in antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody vasculitis
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 62 year old woman with 3 months of sinusitis, epistaxis, saddle nose deformity noted on physical examination, migratory joint pains, and a new 2 week history of haemoptysis with breathlessness. On admission today she has developed rising creatinine and 4 red cell casts on urine microscopy consistent with active glomerulonephritis. She has no fever. Her chest computed tomography demonstrates multiple bilateral nodules with cavitation and patchy alveolar haemorrhage.

Her autoimmune serology returns positive for c-antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody with anti proteinase 3 (PR3) specificity on enzyme linked immunosorbent assay, negative anti myeloperoxidase (MPO), negative anti glomerular basement membrane, negative antinuclear antibody. She has no personal or family history of asthma or eosinophilic disease. She has never smoked.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 148/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 92% on room air, temperature 37.4 degC
data_table.Examination: Saddle nose deformity, crusted nasal mucosa, no rash, bilateral crackles on auscultation, no peripheral neuropathy documented
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 220 micromol/L (baseline 78), urine microscopy 4 red cell casts, c-ANCA/PR3 positive, MPO negative, anti glomerular basement membrane negative, complement C3 and C4 normal, eosinophil count 0.2 x10^9/L

lead_in: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Microscopic polyangiitis with pulmonary renal syndrome, based on the current serological and clinical pattern findings
options.rationale: Microscopic polyangiitis is more commonly p-ANCA/MPO positive and lacks upper airway destructive features such as saddle nose; c-ANCA/PR3 predominance argues against it. (Source: Chapel Hill Consensus Conference nomenclature 2012)
source_refs: Chapel Hill Consensus Conference nomenclature 2012

options.text: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss) based on the current clinical and serological pattern findings
options.rationale: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis requires eosinophilia and asthma; this patient has neither and her serology is c-ANCA/PR3 rather than the more typical p-ANCA/MPO. (Source: Chapel Hill Consensus Conference nomenclature 2012)
source_refs: Chapel Hill Consensus Conference nomenclature 2012

options.text: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener granulomatosis) based on the current clinical and serological pattern findings
options.rationale: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis characteristically presents with upper airway destructive disease (saddle nose, crusted nasal mucosa), pulmonary nodules with cavitation and alveolar haemorrhage, and pauci immune necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis; the serology is c-ANCA/PR3 positive in the majority of cases. (Source: Chapel Hill Consensus Conference nomenclature 2012)
source_refs: Chapel Hill Consensus Conference nomenclature 2012

options.text: Anti glomerular basement membrane disease (Goodpasture syndrome) based on the current clinical and serological pattern findings
options.rationale: Goodpasture syndrome causes alveolar haemorrhage and glomerulonephritis but not sinusitis or saddle nose, and the serology would be anti glomerular basement membrane positive rather than c-ANCA/PR3. (Source: Chapel Hill Consensus Conference nomenclature 2012)
source_refs: Chapel Hill Consensus Conference nomenclature 2012

options.text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with pulmonary renal syndrome, based on the current serological and clinical pattern findings
options.rationale: Systemic lupus erythematosus features low complement, positive antinuclear antibody and typical mucocutaneous features; the c-ANCA/PR3 positive pattern with sinusitis fits granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and the ear nose throat destructive features are not typical of systemic lupus erythematosus. (Source: Chapel Hill Consensus Conference nomenclature 2012)
source_refs: Chapel Hill Consensus Conference nomenclature 2012

explanation.summary: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody associated vasculitis includes granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis typically presents with upper airway destructive disease, lung nodules with cavitation and pauci immune glomerulonephritis; the serology is c-ANCA/PR3 in the majority. Microscopic polyangiitis lacks upper airway destructive disease and is more often p-ANCA/MPO. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis features asthma and eosinophilia. Initial induction therapy for severe granulomatosis with polyangiitis is glucocorticoid plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide, with plasma exchange considered in severe alveolar haemorrhage or rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
key_points: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis: upper airway destructive disease + lung cavitation + pauci immune glomerulonephritis, c-ANCA/PR3 positive.
Microscopic polyangiitis: renal and pulmonary without upper airway features, p-ANCA/MPO positive.
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis requires asthma and eosinophilia.
explanation.pearls: Saddle nose, cavitating lung nodules, pauci immune glomerulonephritis and c-ANCA/PR3 positive is granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener).

sources.label: Chapel Hill Consensus Conference nomenclature 2012
EULAR/ERA-EDTA recommendations for the management of ANCA associated vasculitis

subtopic_detail: Warfarin reversal in ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm needing massive transfusion
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar covering the emergency department at a metropolitan tertiary hospital with vascular surgery on site. A 72 year old man is brought in shocked with sudden severe abdominal and back pain. Point of care ultrasound shows a 7 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm with a large hyperechoic pericaval collection consistent with rupture. He is on warfarin for a previous mechanical mitral valve replacement with target international normalised ratio 2.5 to 3.5. His last known international normalised ratio 4 days ago was 3.2. Massive transfusion protocol has been activated. Vascular surgery is arranging theatre. Anaesthetics and blood bank have been called.

His current international normalised ratio has just come back at 3.6. Fibrinogen has been sent. He is not currently receiving any anticoagulation reversal agent. He is on peripheral fluids and O negative red cells are running. He has no known allergies. Prothrombinex-VF is available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132 /min, blood pressure 78/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 /min, SpO2 94% on 15 L non rebreather, temperature 35.6 degC
data_table.Examination: Pale, mottled peripheries, capillary refill 5 s, abdomen distended and tender with pulsatile mass; peripheral pulses reduced
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 78 g/L (135-175), platelets 168 x10^9/L, international normalised ratio 3.6, activated partial thromboplastin time 42 s, fibrinogen pending, lactate 5.2 mmol/L, base excess -12

lead_in: Which combination is the most appropriate immediate haemostatic strategy in addition to massive transfusion protocol packs?

options.text: Intravenous vitamin K 10 mg alone and wait 6 to 8 hours for the international normalised ratio to fall before theatre today
options.rationale: Vitamin K alone is too slow (6 to 24 hours) for a shocked ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm going to immediate theatre; rapid reversal with a factor concentrate is required. (Source: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guideline)
source_refs: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guideline

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma 4 units alone as the sole reversal agent and hold vitamin K to allow anticoagulation to be resumed post op
options.rationale: Fresh frozen plasma alone is inferior to prothrombin complex concentrate for rapid reversal and delivers a large volume; vitamin K is essential to prevent international normalised ratio rebound and can be given while awaiting mechanical valve restart. (Source: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guideline)
source_refs: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guideline

options.text: Recombinant activated factor VII 90 microg/kg bolus alone with no other reversal adjuncts to control the ruptured aneurysm bleed
options.rationale: Recombinant activated factor VII is off label in this setting, has thrombotic complication risk in the mechanical valve population, and does not replace the missing vitamin K dependent factors as reliably as prothrombin complex concentrate. (Source: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guideline)
source_refs: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guideline

options.text: Intravenous vitamin K 5 to 10 mg plus Prothrombinex-VF 50 units/kg immediately, supplemented by fresh frozen plasma 150 to 300 mL
options.rationale: The National Blood Authority AU pathway for major bleeding on warfarin is immediate intravenous vitamin K 5 to 10 mg plus Prothrombinex-VF 50 units/kg (a three factor concentrate providing II, IX, X) supplemented by fresh frozen plasma to provide factor VII, which is not in the Prothrombinex-VF product. This achieves rapid international normalised ratio reversal while providing all vitamin K dependent factors before theatre. (Source: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guideline)
source_refs: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guideline

options.text: Andexanet alfa 800 mg bolus and infusion regardless of anticoagulant class, to reverse the international normalised ratio before theatre
options.rationale: Andexanet alfa is an antidote to factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban or rivaroxaban, not warfarin; it is inappropriate for warfarin reversal. (Source: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guideline)
source_refs: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guideline

explanation.summary: Immediate warfarin reversal in life threatening haemorrhage uses intravenous vitamin K 5 to 10 mg plus Prothrombinex-VF (a three factor prothrombin complex concentrate containing II, IX and X) 50 units/kg. Because Prothrombinex-VF does not contain factor VII, 150 to 300 mL of fresh frozen plasma is added to provide factor VII. Vitamin K is essential to prevent international normalised ratio rebound after factor concentrate wanes and can be given even with a mechanical heart valve because bridging anticoagulation is available post operatively. Cell salvage, massive transfusion protocol packs with 1:1:1 red cell to fresh frozen plasma to platelet ratio, tranexamic acid 1 g and definitive vascular surgical control complete the strategy. Andexanet alfa is for factor Xa inhibitors, not warfarin.
key_points: Life threatening warfarin bleed: vitamin K 5 to 10 mg intravenously plus Prothrombinex-VF 50 units/kg plus fresh frozen plasma 150 to 300 mL (for factor VII).
Vitamin K prevents international normalised ratio rebound; give even with mechanical valves (bridge post operatively).
Andexanet alfa is for factor Xa inhibitors, not warfarin.
explanation.pearls: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm on warfarin with international normalised ratio 3.6: vitamin K 5 to 10 mg intravenous plus Prothrombinex-VF 50 units/kg plus fresh frozen plasma 150 to 300 mL (for factor VII), alongside the massive transfusion protocol.

sources.label: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guideline
Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: Anticoagulant reversal

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis in Addison disease with concurrent sepsis and vomiting inability to take oral steroid
stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar reviewing a 45 year old woman with known Addison disease of 12 years duration. She usually takes hydrocortisone 20 mg on waking, 10 mg at midday and 5 mg at 5 pm, and fludrocortisone 100 microg on waking. She has been vomiting for 8 hours after a viral gastroenteritis and has not tolerated any oral hydrocortisone today. She has taken her fludrocortisone yesterday. She is now feverish, hypotensive and drowsy. She has not received any parenteral steroid before arrival.

She is under continuous cardiac monitoring. Fluid resuscitation with 0.9 percent saline has started. Blood cultures have been drawn and empirical intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g has been given for suspected sepsis (source not yet clear). Her partner has brought her MedicAlert bracelet and steroid emergency card. The endocrinology registrar has been paged. She has no penicillin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132 /min, blood pressure 78/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 /min, SpO2 96% on 4 L nasal prongs, temperature 38.6 degC
data_table.Examination: Drowsy Glasgow Coma Score 13, mucous membranes dry, cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 s, no focal source of infection on brief examination
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 5.6 mmol/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L, creatinine 118 micromol/L, lactate 3.4 mmol/L, cortisol 30 nmol/L (baseline off treatment reference not applicable)

lead_in: Which single steroid strategy is most appropriate right now?

options.text: Give oral prednisolone 50 mg with an antiemetic now and repeat the same oral prednisolone dose in another hour if required
options.rationale: Oral steroid is inappropriate because she is vomiting and has not tolerated oral medication; parenteral hydrocortisone is required in adrenal crisis. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline for Primary Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline for Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

options.text: Give intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg alone until the endocrinology registrar arrives to review and take over her steroid plan
options.rationale: Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and although it is acceptable when a synacthen test is planned, hydrocortisone is preferred in established Addison disease in crisis because it provides both glucocorticoid and some mineralocorticoid effect at high dose. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline for Primary Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline for Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

options.text: Give intramuscular hydrocortisone 20 mg (her usual morning maintenance dose) intramuscularly as a one off dose today
options.rationale: 20 mg is the maintenance daily first dose; adrenal crisis needs 100 mg intravenous or intramuscular immediately, then 200 mg over 24 hours by infusion or divided doses. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline for Primary Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline for Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

options.text: Continue her usual oral hydrocortisone maintenance dose only and rely on the fludrocortisone dose she took the previous day
options.rationale: Maintenance dosing is inadequate in adrenal crisis, and yesterday's fludrocortisone does not treat today's crisis; parenteral high dose hydrocortisone is required. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline for Primary Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline for Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

options.text: Give intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately then 200 mg over the next 24 hours as an infusion, with saline and glucose
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis management is immediate intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by 200 mg over the following 24 hours (as an infusion or 50 mg intravenously or intramuscularly every 6 hours), together with 0.9 percent saline for volume expansion and correction of hypoglycaemia. Fludrocortisone is not required at this dose because high dose hydrocortisone has enough mineralocorticoid activity. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline for Primary Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline for Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is treated with immediate intravenous or intramuscular hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by 200 mg over the next 24 hours (as an infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours), 0.9 percent saline volume expansion and correction of hypoglycaemia. Fludrocortisone is not required at these hydrocortisone doses because of sufficient mineralocorticoid effect; it is reintroduced when the daily hydrocortisone falls below 50 mg. Precipitants (in this case gastroenteritis and possible sepsis) are treated concurrently. Sick day rules and a steroid emergency card should be reviewed with the patient after recovery. If the diagnosis of primary adrenal insufficiency is not established, dexamethasone is preferred initially so a subsequent synacthen test is not confounded.
key_points: Adrenal crisis: intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately, then 200 mg over 24 hours (or 50 mg every 6 hours).
Fludrocortisone is not needed at these hydrocortisone doses; reintroduce when daily hydrocortisone falls below 50 mg.
Dexamethasone is preferred if a synacthen test is planned and diagnosis is unconfirmed.
explanation.pearls: Adrenal crisis in known Addison: intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg now, then 200 mg over 24 hours, plus 0.9 percent saline and glucose correction.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline for Primary Adrenal Insufficiency
Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Adrenal disorders
